                             STATEMENT     BY     LAWRENCE   EDWARD    BARRY

                                                I remember the 23rd February 1974 .       On
            the 22nd February 1974 , Friday, I had travelled to Iffley Station
                •
                                                                                               ,



           at approximately 6 . 00 p . m.             The purpose for this particular trip
           was to water test a six inch Bore which required testing for
           twenty- four hours straight with tests taken every half hour. .                     The

                                                - UNUSU.AL il.ERIAL SIGHTINGS
                               -INVESTIGATION'S
                                   PROPOSED CH.ANGES TO REPORTING FORMS


            1.        Investigations of unusual aerial sightings have, in many cases,
            been prolonged because of inadequate quGstions and detailed description
            from investigating officers and witnesses . Causes for these insufficiencies
            are thought to be:

                        a.     lack of expertise of investigating officer;

                        b.     lack of motivation, interest or time , expr essed
                               by or available to the investigating officer; and

                        c.     insufficient direction avai:iable on the r eporting
                               proformao .

            2.        In an endeavour to upgr ade the standard of investigations into
            these sightings, r evised proformae have been dra£ted, and are a ttached as
            4nnex A. Comments arc requestBd from Bases af ter collation of formation/
            unit comments, on the suitability of , or r eccIIUU.ended changes to , the draft
            forms .

            3.        This ro quire~ent is to be actioned so that comoents are returned to
            this headquarters by 22nd June 1973.

            Dear Sir,
                          RE:-SIGHTING OF UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECT.

                            I wish to report that at 6.38.P.M. on Friday
            the 18th June 1971, an unidentified flying object wae sighted
            in the sky by residents of Burketown, Queenelando
                                 ( 1) ••• To the naked eye the object resembled
                                 an ill11mjnoue cigar shaped object (pointed
                                 at both ends);    at first it took on an orange
                                 into red colour and lastly a clear light colour;
                                 it seemed to be about eight feet long.
                                 (2) ••• It was sighted west of Burketown on the
                                  southern side of the setting sun in a clear
                                  sky and good weather conditions; the sunset
                                  created a red glow along the horizon for some
                                  distance.
                                  ( 3) . .. . - It travelled from north to south
                                  along and above the horizon at what appeared
                                  to be a height of 30-40 feet;          it moved qnly
                                  slowly across the sky, then seemed to become
                                 'stationary momentarily, then lose altitude
                                  before changing to an easterly course towards
                                  Burketown for a £ew minutes. before again
                                  changing course towards the· south-west in which
                                  direction it disappeared.
                                  ( 4)... It was sighted at 6. 38. P. M. and
                                  disappeared at about 6.55.P.M.
                                 (5) ••• The first sighting of the object was
                                 made by Mrs. Ivy McDERMOTT, a housewife of                  ·
                                 Burketown, who telephoned the local Post-Master-
                                 Mr. Albert Percy LEE who together with his
                                 wife Mrs. Ivy LEE then sighted the object as
                                 described;   Other persons were then either
                                 pnoned by the Poet-Master or phoned him
                                 confirming the sighting some of their names
                                 being:- Dieter JORDAN, Grazier, of Bu.rketown,
                                 Dawson HUMBLE, Shire Clerk of Burketown, Mrso
                                 Gwen JOYNER, housewife of Burketown;& Mr.
                                 Alfred HORNE, Storekeeper, of Burketown.
                 The circumstances of the sighting are regarded as unusual
            and cannot be explained here.   I request your opinion as
            to what this particular unidentified flying object may have beene
            Newspaper cutting on this sighting is at t ached.
                  I   am a member of the Naval Coastwatching Organisationo

      AIRCRAFT MENACEV AT GOO::J1W1NV1 AIRPORT - CEI. - 10/9/11            f/f
         The reporter,Mr. H. is an experienced aircraft engineer who
         at the time of the incident was travelling as a passenger on
         a B.P.A. trilander flying from Cunnamulla - Brisbane via
         Goondiwindi.                                                                •
         The aircraft had completed the first leg of the trip and was
         to land at Goondiwindi airport and pick up passengers, due to
 . , .. engine matenance the flight had been delayed and the time was
         now approximately 03.00 hrs.
         Mr. H. was sitting next to the pilot of the trilander. Within
         a short distance of the airport Mr. H. and the pilot noticed
         what they first thought to be another aircraft approaching on
         a similar but opposite course.
         While still on final approach to the airport the pilot confirmed
       · through Air Traffic Control (Brisbane and Sydney) that no other
         aircraft 'should be in .the area.
         The pilot, Mr. H., and another passenger (also a pilot) discussed
         for a few moments what the approaching lights may have been.
       With the B.P.A. aircraft and the "unknown" on what appeared
       to be an eventual colliaion co~rse, the pilot took evasive
       action and turned the· trilander away from its approach to the
       airport. Mr. H • .sitting on the (right hand side) starboard

      Be this as it may, we must still remember that all human
      experiences are affected by certain preconceived ideas ·
      and images. The veiwing of U.F.O. type science fiction/
      factual movies and television programs may put a different
                                                                       \
                                                                                ..
      slant on these ideas, and hence influence the way the
      witness interperates a tJ.F.O .. incident he or she may become ...        •
      involved in.
      This is for the most part an unconcious reaction, and in
      the case of hoaxes a concious one. So the investigator
      must weed out any effect such mass media has had.
      To this end there is one question that should be added
      to the Australian U.F.O. Report form, (to be placed after
      "Have you read any U.F.O. literature"). The question should
      read "Have you seen any U.F.O. type science fiction motion
      picture or T.V. programs recently" and "if so what were
      they?"
       The media influence could then be taken into account.
       Movement, shape, colour, tactics etc of the U.F.O. can then
       be compared with those in the movie, and details of the
       report can be checked against the plot of the movie to see
       if there is any degree of similarity.
       This means of course more work for the investigators, but
       also more accurate data. Remember art mimics life, but
       life also mimics art. Be warned, with millions of veiwers
       enjoying sci-Fiction films the concious and subconcious
       minds of the population of this planet are being primed for
       a new burst of U.F.O. stories.
       Here come the "Unidenifiable Fraudulant Objects".
       REF: U.F.O.'s Reel Vs Real; James E. Oberg. Starlog No. 12
       March, 1978.

                           The investigation of reports of U . ~' . O . s in Australia is carried
                                                                                                       •
                 out by the Royal Australian Air Force , Directorate of Air Force
                 Intelligence , at the Department of Air in Canberra.            A considerable amount
                 of effort is spent in investigatin~ each r epo rt a nd the majority of
                 observers are interviewed by selected R.l. •. '.1. . F . personnel.

                            Bet·weon 23rd Jro1t1ary 1960 and 30th December 1971, the R .J.1. . f.1. . F .
                 received 595 U. F . O. reports .   Department of Air has assessed that 93
                 percent were explainable by present scientific knowledge .      Six percent
                 of the r epor ts did not provide sufficient information to permit proper
                 analysis and evaluation .      Once percent of the reports were attributed to
                 unknown causes .

                           The Uni ted Kingdom Air Ministry has stated that on an average ,
                 90 percent of the sightings i t invostigateo are explainable by causes
                 ranging from meteorological balloons and meteors to aircraft lights .   The
                 other 10 9ercent probably remain unexplained because of lack of reliable
                 information.

                            In 1966 the University of Colorado , under contract to the U. S.A. F.,
                 spent two years processing and investigat ing all !...:merican reports .     Its
                 findings have been published by Bantam Books as the ' Condon Report '.         Its
                 general conclusion is that ' nothing has come from the study of U. F . O. s
                 in the past 21 years that he.s added to sc:= r.>ntifi c knowledge ' and that
                 ' further extensive study of U. F . O. s probably cannot be justified in the
                 expectation that sci ence will be advanced tbereby '.       A panel of eminent
                 scientists, chosen by t~e U. S. National ~cademy of Sciences , has examined
                 and endorsed the Condon Report .

                           The U. S. A. F . ' Project Blue Book ' investigation of unidentified
                 aerial objects between 1953 and 1965 analysed 7 , 641 U. F . O. r eports .
                 It concluded that :

                             a.    80 percent of sightings were natural pl1enomena,
                                   hoaxes , birds or man- made objects ;

                             b.    17 persent of sightings provid~d insufficient data
                                   to permit thorough analysis a~d ev~luation ; and

                             c.    thre e percent were unidentified .

                             U. S. and Soviet space exploration ha.s f ound no evidence to support
                 tl1e theory of life on planets in our solar system.         It seems that the ~1arinc, r
                 series of space explor at ion to Mars has proved it a ' dead ' planet .      The only
                 other source of e7tra- terrestrial life , then , would have to be in another
                 ' sola.r system 1 •  It would seem, tl1erefore , thu t \<thilst it may be possibl e for
                 extr a- t8rre strial life forms to visit Earth, it is improbable .

                 Austr alia between January 1960 and December 1971.

          This light was seen three knights in succession. The first
          two nights, following a ,s jmilar pattern appearing west south
          west of my home and moving up and down, and from side to s~e
          gradually moving away in a south westerley direction, with an
          exception that on the second night we saw a pale red or pink
          light at the bottom    op
                                 the larger bright light.
          On the third night the light hovered more or less in the same
          area for about twenty minutes. During this time I was able to
          borrow a: pair of' binocular,s which gave us a clearer view o'I
          the object which seemed crystal shaped with a long narrow
          shadow on the right hand side reaching nearly to the centre
          of the light. The shadow later moved more to the top of the
          light but, still on the right hand side.
          At intervals only,a smaller round light appeared from behind
          the larger light on the bottom left hand corner, moving away
          from and then returning towards the larger light, sometimes
          dissapearing completely behind the larger light, moving much
          faster than the larger light.
          This smaller light was a bright pink in colour and the size
          of the sammer light was like a ping-pong ball beside a foot-
          ball in comparison wi.th the larger light.
          Af'ter about twenty minutes, the larger yellow light moved
          away in a similar pattern as the two previous night,s , leaving
          no trace of the smaller pink li~t.
